questions.prompt: What scorecard correction does Chapter 7 make first?
choices: Continuity automatically proves discipline
Family control removes the need for hard tradeoffs
Protected continuity still has to earn trust under a scorecard

explanation.gentle: The chapter starts by refusing to treat continuity as proof by itself.
explanation.direct: Thorndike challenges the idea that family-linked stability already counts as stewardship.

questions.prompt: Why does a family-control setting create pressure in this chapter?
choices: Because family influence can preserve patience but also soften accountability
Because family firms never think long term
Because continuity ends all allocation problems

explanation.gentle: The same protection that creates patience can also make weak habits harder to challenge.
explanation.direct: Family control changes incentives in both useful and risky ways.
explanation.competitive: The shelter can protect strength or hide weakness.

questions.prompt: What does optimization mean in this chapter?
choices: Improving the enterprise without worshipping either disruption or tradition
Keeping everything the family already prefers
Choosing dramatic reinvention to prove courage

explanation.gentle: Optimization means making the firm better inside continuity rather than treating continuity as untouchable.
explanation.direct: The chapter defines optimization as disciplined improvement under ownership constraints.
explanation.competitive: The point is a stronger company, not prettier loyalty or louder rebellion.

questions.prompt: Lila sees legacy routines surviving because of history. What fits Chapter 7 best?
choices: Preserve all of them because continuity matters most
Test the routines against the work they still improve
Replace every old habit immediately to prove change

explanation.gentle: The chapter says continuity deserves respect only when it keeps helping the enterprise.
explanation.direct: Choice B matches Smith's logic: optimization audits the protected habits instead of worshipping or destroying them automatically.
explanation.competitive: Make the history win on merit.

questions.prompt: Which belief does Chapter 7 challenge most directly?
choices: Family control is always wise
Optimization means avoiding hard choices
Both A and B

explanation.gentle: The chapter rejects easy praise of family control and easy softness disguised as optimization.
explanation.direct: Thorndike pushes against romanticizing the structure and against using continuity as cover for weak decisions.
explanation.competitive: Dynasty worship and conflict avoidance both fail here.

questions.prompt: Connor sees the student paper protecting a slow routine because it feels traditional. What is the chapter's best diagnosis?
choices: The routine deserves protection because it is part of the identity
The group is letting continuity grade itself instead of auditing it
The only rational move is to reject every tradition

explanation.gentle: The group is protecting the routine before checking whether it still helps the mission.
explanation.direct: This is Chapter 7 in miniature: insulation is softening the scorecard.
explanation.competitive: The tradition is collecting respect without earning it.

questions.prompt: Why is the anti-insulation rule necessary here?
choices: Because protected structures can let weak tradeoffs survive too long
Because family influence eliminates emotional pressure
Because continuity should always be broken quickly

explanation.gentle: Protection can make it easier for weak choices to keep surviving.
explanation.direct: The chapter needs anti-insulation discipline because social and emotional shelter can blur accountability.

questions.prompt: What limit keeps Chapter 7 from becoming a romantic family-business story?
choices: Continuity only deserves respect when it improves stewardship and allocation
Family control always creates superior patience
Optimization means never questioning protected units

explanation.gentle: The chapter stays strict by asking whether the protected structure still makes the business better.
explanation.direct: Family control earns respect only when discipline remains stronger than insulation.
explanation.competitive: Sentiment loses when the scorecard gets serious.

questions.prompt: What makes Smith's continuity rational in Thorndike's frame?
choices: The family structure itself guarantees good stewardship
Continuity is forced to improve the enterprise instead of merely preserving it
The chapter avoids judging capital allocation directly

explanation.gentle: The continuity matters only because it still has to produce a better business.
explanation.direct: Thorndike makes stewardship quality, not structure alone, the evidence that counts.
explanation.competitive: The firm has to get better, not just stay familiar.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 7 prepare the move toward Buffett in Chapter 8?
choices: It proves ownership structure no longer matters at all
It shows disciplined allocation surviving inside family control before Buffett makes investor logic the operating center
It argues continuity is more important than capital allocation

explanation.gentle: Smith keeps allocation discipline alive inside family control before Buffett clarifies it further in Berkshire.
explanation.direct: Chapter 7 tests rationality under protected continuity, then Chapter 8 makes investor-operator logic more explicit.
explanation.competitive: First continuity gets disciplined, then allocation becomes the whole operating brain.
